extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and enthusiasts of architecture and architectural criticism (interested in Gothic/Venetian architecture)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and critical tests for determining whether a building is 'good Gothic' (and whether, beyond style-purity, it is good architecture), with specific attention to Venetian Gothic palaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roof rises in a steep gable
rubrics_metrics.description: Look if the roof rises in a steep gable, high above the walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it does not do this, 'the building is not quite pure Gothic, or has been altered.' This is presented as the first and simplest test for Gothic purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal windows and doors have pointed arches with gables
rubrics_metrics.description: Look if the principal windows and doors have pointed arches with gables over them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not pointed arches, 'the building is not Gothic'; if they have no gables over them, 'it is either not pure, or not first-rate.' If steep roof, pointed arches, and gable are all united, 'it is nearly certain to be a Gothic building of a very fine time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Arches are cusped or apertures foliated (foliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look if the arches are cusped, or apertures foliated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the building met the first two conditions it is 'sure to be foliated somewhere'; but if foliation is missing 'anywhere, the building is assuredly imperfect Gothic.' Exception: large bearing arches or small sharp grouped arches that form a kind of foliation by multiplicity, and elements relieved by sculpture and rich mouldings, may be acceptable. (Example: some upper windows of Westminster Abbey are imperfect for want of foliation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Arches carried on true shafts with bases and capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Look if its arches in general, whether of windows and doors or minor ornamentation, are carried on true shafts with bases and capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If they are, 'the building is assuredly of the finest Gothic style.' If apertures have no shafts and capitals but are 'plain openings in the walls, studiously simple, and unmoulded at the sides,' the building may still be of the finest Gothic adapted to domestic or military service. But if the sides of the window are moulded and yet there are no capitals at the spring of the arch, 'it is assuredly of an inferior school.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentiality of composition (nothing superfluous)
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition from which anything can be removed without doing mischief is always so far forth inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle as a general test of artistic quality: elements should be essential to the whole; gratuitous or removable ornament indicates inferiority of style or execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of workmanship: 'built by strong men' vs excessive precision
rubrics_metrics.description: See if the building 'looks as if it had been built by strong men' — having roughness, largeness, and nonchalance mixed with exquisite tenderness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This character is favorable and indicates a noble building. If wholly accurate, minute, and scrupulous in workmanship, it likely belongs to either the very best (exquisite design) or the very worst (mechanism replacing design); on balance, 'very accurate workmanship is to be esteemed a bad sign' and mere precision without remark may be passed with contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregularity of parts (irregularity as a positive sign)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe if the building is irregular, its different parts fitting themselves to different purposes, no one caring what becomes of them, so that they do their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one part always answers accurately to another part it is 'sure to be a bad building'; conspicuous irregularities often indicate a master's daring and a good building (example: Ducal Palace windows/arcade offsets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual variety in traceries, capitals, and ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe if all the traceries, capitals, and other ornaments are of perpetually varied design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not perpetually varied, 'the work is assuredly bad.' Variety of detail is a criterion of good Gothic workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture must be legible and properly scaled
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the sculpture: first discover whether it is legible; on a good building the sculpture is set and on such a scale that at the ordinary distance the sculpture shall be thoroughly intelligible and interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To accomplish legibility, uppermost statues will be ten or twelve feet high, and upper ornamentation 'colossal,' increasing in fineness as it descends, often worked as if for a precious cabinet at the foundation. The spectator should be able to 'see them plainly, and make them all out at his ease.' After this, the criticism proceeds as on a book and depends on the reader's knowledge, feeling, industry and perseverance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization/gradation of ornament (Byzantine vs Gothic indication of date)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether groups of windows/capitals show a centralization where the midmost piece is superior to the rest (a Byzantine trait retained in early Gothic), or whether capitals are all different or all alike (a later trait).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In early groups of five lights the midmost capital is different from the two on each side; whenever capitals are not centralized (either entirely alike, or all different with no correspondence), 'it is a certain proof ... of the comparative lateness of the building.' The Ducal Palace breaks this system (capitals all different) and so appears later in this respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break-up of continuous arcades into definite windows and doors (form of Gothic palaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic palaces break long continuous Byzantine arcades into central and lateral windows and small arched doors; e.g., sea story of a Gothic palace consists of a door and one or two windows on each side; first story of a Gothic palace consists of a central window of four or five lights with single windows on each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change in general form—from unified continuous arcades to discrete, centralized window-door composition—is a diagnostic sign of Gothic adaptation to domestic architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceries as structural elements; proper scale and masonry joints
rubrics_metrics.description: In Venetian Gothic, the traceries of the windows often support the building; traceries are enormously increased in scale and thickness when they must bear superincumbent weight; details like the placement of the quatrefoil and the positions of horizontal joints reflect structural logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether traceries are appropriately scaled and jointed to bear load (e.g., moving the quatrefoil between arches to throw bearing power between them rather than under). Structural function of traceries (not merely decorative glass support) is a positive trait in Venice; incorrect or decorative-only traceries imply fragility or imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of materials, facings, string courses and angle treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic palaces show gradual removal of marble facings from walls, with bare brick or stucco contrasted against marble shafts and archivolts; stories divided by bold, decorated string courses; angles chamfered and filled by small twisted shafts with capitals under each story-cornice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features contribute to the building's appearance of firmness while maintaining lightness of form—important in Venice because of foundation insecurity. The twisted angle shafts (diminishing upwards, ringed with dog-tooth ornament) visually 'bind' walls and reassure stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parapets and roof-crowns should be ornamental, crown-like, and appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Roof parapets in Venetian Gothic are purely ornamental, crown-like ornaments (not true battlements or machicolations); palace parapets are lighter and more fantastic—narrow lance-like spires and fleur-de-lis (lily) forms—often finished with gilded balls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect parapets chiefly on courts/gardens or to crown important façades; their form and scale should be appropriate to location (not fortress-like), and their delicate forms help 'relieve' the mass below. Misplaced or heavy battlement-like parapets indicate other (non-Venetian Gothic or inappropriate) influence.
